title: How do you build a training matrix for a shipping company?
seoTitle: Training matrix for a shipping company
description: Build a shipping company training matrix: STCW revalidation, ISM familiarization, MLC, ISPS drills and port State control evidence by flag, rank and ship.
shortAnswer: A shipping company training matrix is built by listing every shipboard rank and shore role (master, officers, ratings, cooks, security officers, the designated person ashore, crewing managers) against the instruments that bind each ship: STCW, the ISM Code, the Maritime Labour Convention, the ISPS Code and the rules of each flag State. Each cell records the clock, such as five year revalidation or three monthly security drills, and the evidence a port State inspector or auditor will examine.
keyTakeaways: Shipping obligations attach to the flag a ship flies, the capacity a seafarer serves in and the ship type, so the matrix needs flag and ship dimensions that a shore based matrix lacks.

Four IMO and ILO instruments form the baseline everywhere: STCW for competence, ISM section 6 for familiarization and company training, MLC Regulation 1.3 for qualification and personal safety, and the ISPS Code for security roles and drills.

Several clocks are fixed: STCW basic training competence shown every five years, EU medical certificates valid for at most two years, ISPS drills every three months and exercises no more than 18 months apart.
Port State control can test competence at the place of duty, so evidence must show a named seafarer could do the job, not only that a certificate exists.
Watch dates as at November 2026 include the 2025 MLC amendments, expected to enter into force on 23 December 2027, and the ongoing comprehensive review of STCW.

sections.heading: Why does a shipping company need its own kind of training matrix?

blocks.text: Because a seafarer's training obligations depend on which flag the ship flies, what capacity they serve in and what kind of ship it is, and those facts change with every contract. A shore matrix keyed to job titles cannot show that a second officer moving from an Australian flagged tanker to an EU flagged ro-ro vessel picks up new familiarization and certificate recognition duties.

The method in [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) still applies: people down one side, obligations across the top, a rule in each cell. A shipping company adds three dimensions: the flag State whose rules govern the certificate, the ship or ship type a person is assigned to, and the port States the ship calls at. Treat masters, watchkeeping officers and security officers as [safety critical roles](/glossary/safety-critical-role) whose currency gates crew assignment.

The company also carries obligations of its own. Under the [ISM Code](/regulations/ism-code-personnel-and-training-requirements), it is the company, not the seafarer, that must man each ship with qualified, certificated and medically fit seafarers and give new and transferred personnel familiarization before they take up safety duties.

sections.heading: Which training rules apply to a shipping company in each market?

blocks.text: Columns come from the international instruments that bind every covered ship, then from each flag State's implementing rules, then from the port States the ship calls at. Each summary below draws only on the linked regulation page.

items: **Every flag, competence.** The STCW Convention requires basic training in four areas set out in section A-VI/1 of the STCW Code: personal survival techniques, fire prevention and firefighting, elementary first aid, and personal safety and social responsibilities. Since the Manila amendments, in force on 1 January 2012, seafarers must show every five years that they have maintained that competence ([STCW seafarer training](/regulations/stcw-seafarer-training-requirements)).

**Every flag, safety management.** ISM Code section 6, mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX, requires familiarization for new and transferred personnel before safety duties begin, training identified by the safety management system, and information in a working language the crew understands. The Document of Compliance and Safety Management Certificate each run for up to five years, with annual and intermediate verification ([ISM Code](/regulations/ism-code-personnel-and-training-requirements)).

**Ratifying flags, labor standards.** Regulation 1.3 of the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 says seafarers shall not work on a ship unless trained or certified as competent and trained for personal safety on board, and training under STCW counts for both. Australia, Japan and Portugal have ratified; the United States and the United Arab Emirates have not ([Maritime Labour Convention](/regulations/maritime-labour-convention-training-and-qualifications)).

**Every flag, security.** The ISPS Code requires company, ship and port facility security officers to have knowledge and training, and personnel with security duties to be able to perform them. Part B sets drills at least every three months and exercises at least once each calendar year with no more than 18 months between them; Regulation (EC) No 725/2004 and 33 CFR 104.230 make those intervals binding in the EU and the United States ([ISPS Code](/regulations/isps-code-ship-and-port-security-training)).

**EU flags.** Directive (EU) 2022/993 codifies STCW for ships flying a Member State flag. Article 15 makes the company responsible for crew certificates and ship specific familiarization, Article 12 limits medical certificates to two years (one year under 18), and Article 13 sets revalidation at intervals not exceeding five years ([EU seafarer training directive](/regulations/eu-port-state-control-and-seafarer-training-directive)).

**United States flag.** The US Coast Guard applies STCW basic training through 46 CFR 11.302 and 12.602, and vessel security officers need an STCW endorsement requiring age 18, an accepted course and qualifying sea service, and must maintain a TWIC.

**Australian domestic commercial vessels.** Marine Order 505 (2022) sets 14 kinds of certificate of competency, each needing a minimum age of 16, a current HLTAID011 first aid certificate and medical fitness. Marine Order 504 (2024), in force since 1 June 2025, requires induction, familiarization and emergency training before duties begin, risk based drills, and records kept for 5 years ([AMSA domestic commercial vessels](/regulations/amsa-domestic-commercial-vessel-crew-requirements)).

**US shore operations handling hazardous materials.** Under 49 CFR 172.704, hazmat employees, including office staff who classify goods or complete shipping papers, are trained within 90 days and retrained at least every three years, with mode specific additions in Parts 174 to 177 ([DOT hazmat training](/regulations/dot-hazmat-employee-training)).

sections.heading: Which shipping intervals are fixed by rule and which does the company set?

blocks.text: Certificate, medical and security drill intervals are mostly fixed by rule, while the content and timing of training identified under the safety management system are left to the company. Record the source of each interval so a flag State auditor can tell a legal limit from an internal choice.

items: **Fixed by rule.** Five yearly evidence of STCW basic training competence; EU revalidation at intervals not exceeding five years; EU medical certificates valid for at most two years; Australian seafarer certificates under Marine Order 70 expiring five years after issue; ISPS drills every three months and exercises no more than 18 months apart; ISM internal audits at intervals not exceeding twelve months; three yearly US hazmat retraining.

**Event triggered.** ISM familiarization before safety duties for new and transferred personnel; ISPS drills within one week when more than 25% of the crew changes; US vessel drills within one week of reactivation. Model these as triggers on crew change and assignment, not as calendar dates.

**Sea service can replace a course.** In the United States, one year of sea service in the last five years is accepted for listed basic training elements. In Australia, Marine Order 73 accepts 12 months of sea service in five years, or three months in the last six, with maintained competence. The matrix must record which route each seafarer used.

**Left to the company.** ISM section 6 requires the company to identify and provide the training its safety management system needs, without an interval, and Marine Order 504 drills follow a risk based schedule. Document the rationale as described in [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: What evidence will flag States, auditors and port State control ask for?

blocks.text: Expect to show that a named seafarer on a named ship was competent and familiarized for their duties, not just that a certificate was issued. Maritime inspections combine document review with interviews and, in port State control, a demonstration at the place of duty.

items: **ISM audits.** IMO Resolution A.1118(30) directs auditors to gather objective evidence through interviews and document examination, with observation where necessary. Familiarization checklists, training identified by the safety management system and verification of delegated crewing tasks are typical samples.

**Port State control.** Under Articles 23 to 25 of Directive (EU) 2022/993, officers check certificates, may assess a seafarer's ability to demonstrate competence at the place of duty where there are clear grounds, and may detain a ship on six listed grounds. MLC Article V(7) means ships of non-ratifying States receive no more favorable treatment in ratifying ports.

**Security records.** US vessel and facility records are kept for at least 2 years; training records include date, duration, description and attendees, and drill records include lessons learned (33 CFR 104.235 and 105.225).
**Australian domestic vessels.** Marine Order 504 requires training and drill records kept for 5 years and a crew list showing certificates.
**Hazmat.** 49 CFR 172.704(d) requires a record of the preceding three years with name, completion date, materials, trainer name and address, and certification of training and testing.
A broader checklist is in [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: Which shipping training changes should be dated in the matrix?

blocks.text: Add these as dated rows so affected cells change on the right day. Each date comes from the linked regulation pages, as at November 2026.

items: **23 June 2027:** the disagreement period for the 2025 MLC amendments ends. The amendments add shipboard violence and harassment provisions to Standard A4.3 and guidance on medical training guides.

**23 December 2027:** expected entry into force of the 2025 MLC amendments for ratifying States, which affects induction and welfare content for crews on Australian, Japanese and Portuguese flagged ships.

**2029 to 2030:** target completion of the IMO comprehensive review of STCW, which identified more than 400 gaps in February 2025. HTW 12, held 23 to 27 February 2026, began phase 2 with chapters II and III.

blocks.title: Already in force
blocks.text: Marine Order 504 (2024) replaced the 2018 order on 1 June 2025, introducing new safety management system requirements for all Australian domestic commercial vessels. Marine Order 70 was last amended by the Marine Orders Miscellaneous Amendment Order 2026 (No. 2) from 1 April 2026.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records each maritime obligation with the flag, ship type and capacity it belongs to, and links it to the learning outcomes and assessment points that show a seafarer is competent and familiarized. When an instrument is amended, such as the 2025 MLC changes or a revised STCW chapter, the affected rows and materials are flagged for review. See [operational procedures](/programs/operational-procedures).

faqs.q: Does the Maritime Labour Convention matter for a US flagged ship?
faqs.a: Yes, in practice. The United States has not ratified the MLC, but Article V(7) says ships of non-ratifying States receive no more favorable treatment when inspected in the ports of ratifying States. A US flagged ship calling at Australian, Japanese or Portuguese ports should be able to evidence Regulation 1.3 qualification and personal safety training.

faqs.q: Does STCW training also satisfy MLC Regulation 1.3?
faqs.a: Largely, yes. The MLC states that training and certification under IMO instruments such as STCW counts as meeting the requirements to be competent for duties and trained for personal safety. Ships' cooks are an exception worth a separate column, because Standard A3.2 sets its own training and qualification standard for them.

faqs.q: Should ISPS drills be tracked per person or per ship?
faqs.a: Both. The three monthly drill and annual exercise clocks belong to the ship, but the one week trigger when more than 25% of the crew changes depends on who has joined. Track drills against the ship and record each participant so crew turnover can fire the trigger automatically.

faqs.q: Do domestic vessels need the same matrix as international ships?
faqs.a: Not in Australia. Domestic commercial vessels fall under the national law, with certificates of competency under Marine Order 505 and safety management under Marine Order 504. Class 1 to 3 vessels may instead follow ISM Code Part A with specified additions, so record which route each vessel uses.
